title: Rolling, blue-green or canary?

rows.label: In one line
values: Replace instances a batch at a time
Build a second environment, then switch all traffic to it
Give the new version a small share of traffic, then widen it

rows.label: Extra capacity
values: None to one batch, depending on surge settings
A full second copy during the release (ECS warns it may double resource use)
A few extra instances, or none if the platform splits traffic between versions

rows.label: Rollback speed
values: Slow: another rollout, batch by batch
Seconds: switch the router back, while the old side is still running
Fast: set the canary’s weight to 0

rows.label: Versions live at once
values: Two, mixed, for the length of the rollout
One serving traffic; both running until the old side is scaled down
Two, side by side, for the whole rollout

rows.label: Blast radius of a bad release
values: Each batch that passes health checks; a bug that health checks miss reaches everyone
Everyone, from the moment of the switch until you switch back
Only the canary’s share, if you catch it before widening

rows.label: What it needs
values: Several instances, health checks or readiness probes, backward-compatible changes
Room for two environments, a switchable router or DNS, schema changes split into expand and contract
Weighted routing, good metrics compared against the stable version, enough traffic for a signal

rows.label: Best for
values: Everyday releases of stateless services; the default strategy of a Kubernetes Deployment
Releases that need instant rollback or can’t run mixed for long
High-traffic services where a regression must reach as few users as possible

rows.label: Built into
values: Kubernetes Deployments, ECS, EC2 Auto Scaling instance refresh, VM Scale Sets
ECS, CodeDeploy, App Service slots, Argo Rollouts
Lambda aliases, API Gateway, Cloud Run, CodeDeploy, ECS, Argo Rollouts, Flagger

tip: Start with rolling deployments; they are the default for a reason and cost nothing extra. Add blue-green when a slow rollback would hurt more than paying for a second environment, and canaries when you have the traffic and the metrics to judge a new version on a slice of users. They combine: Amazon ECS canary deployments shift traffic between a blue and a green revision, and many teams canary first and then roll the rest. All three keep two versions alive for a while, so database changes still need expand and contract.
